title: Apply new rules prospectively
primary_topics: San Roque Power VAT-refund doctrinal column June 9, 2013 -- sequel to B19 (May 26) JFC-pained-letter introduction; same FDI-trust thesis extended via Civil Code Article 4 + retroactive-rule-change doctrine
Q1 first-quarter 7.8% giant economic leap -- World Bank + MAP (top business executives) called for conversion of 'naked growth' to 'inclusive growth' (alleviates poverty + creates jobs for masses)

MAP-JFC joint advocacy: government must 'honor its commitments to regain its credibility and trustworthiness'; CJP back-references his column two weeks ago (B19): trustworthiness reason FDIs trickle to PH but pour to Malaysia/Thailand/Singapore/Indonesia/neighbors

FDIs-vs-hot-money distinction: FDIs 'rooted in and stay for many decades in basic industries that spur inclusive growth'; promote prosperity of both rich and poor, capital and labor, entrepreneurs and masses; hot money 'invested short term, like stock market, bonds or bank deposits that can flee as fast as they come in'; FDIs are 'long-term commitments' that 'cannot be withdrawn instantly'; hot money 'not necessarily bad; helps expansion of existing businesses and normally precedes the more desirable FDIs'
JFC's solution: 'Honor commitments. Don't change rules midstream'; MAP added that if rules change, new rules should be 'applied prospectively so as not to prejudice existing investments'

San Roque Power case-study: 1990s electric-power-outages context; Japanese investors led by Marubeni formed San Roque Power Corp.; imported machinery to generate ~400MW; government promise of VAT-exemption; at that time '$1 million to generate one megawatt' (now doubled to $2M/MW)

Procedural detail: San Roque first required to pay VAT then apply for refund at BIR; RA 8424 -- application filed in BIR; if BIR rejects or fails to act within 120 days, 30-day appeal window to CTA; otherwise VAT refund forfeited

San Roque timeline: BIR refund application March 28, 2003; even before lapse of 120 days, filed judicial claim in CTA April 10, 2003; 'accepted practice at that time -- to undergo both administrative refund process in BIR and judicial process in CTA simultaneously, instead of successively'; simultaneous filing justified because at that time 'law also required judicial claims for refund to be filed within two years from submission of VAT returns'; allowed in at least 20 previous refund cases; once simultaneous CTA recourse availed of, BIR suspended own processing

Litigation course: CTA granted San Roque VAT refund; BIR appealed (unlike previous cases where BIR simply accepted CTA decisions); Jan 12, 2011 First Division of SC unanimously dismissed appeal + ordered BIR to refund; BIR motion for reconsideration; Feb 12 (2013) Court en banc split-decision reversed First Division -- San Roque should have first waited 120-day BIR lapse before filing CTA; San Roque MR still pending

CJP's policy prescription via Article 4 of Civil Code: 'Laws shall have no retroactive effect, unless the contrary is provided' in law itself; JFC + MAP not contesting wisdom of new decision -- 'merely asking that it be applied prospectively to new refund applications, but not to San Roque and other similarly situated companies, which followed the old practice'; CJP-endorsement: 'this stance is reasonable, fair and equitable... To show good faith, earn confidence of investors and ultimately spread fruits of our stunning economic growth with the poor, the government should heed the call of the World Bank, MAP and JFC'

World Bank and Management Association of Philippines (MAP), organization of top business executives of country
Called for conversion of this naked growth to inclusive growth
One that alleviates poverty and creates jobs for our masses
To do that, MAP joined Joint Foreign Chambers (JFC) in urging our government to honor its commitments
To regain its credibility and trustworthiness
In this space two weeks ago, CJP opined that trustworthiness is reason FDIs have come in trickles to Philippines
But have been poured massively on Malaysia, Thailand, Singapore, Indonesia and other neighbors
FDIs are desired everywhere because, unlike 'hot money,' they are rooted in and stay for many decades in basic industries
That spur inclusive growth
Yes, inclusive growth, not just naked economic growth, is goal of all countries
Because it promotes prosperity of both rich and poor, both capital and labor, both entrepreneurs and masses
Hot money is invested short term, like in stock market, bonds or bank deposits that can flee as fast as they come in
FDIs are long-term commitments; once invested, they cannot be withdrawn instantly
Hot money is not necessarily bad; it helps in expansion of existing businesses and normally precedes the more desirable FDIs
To attract FDIs, JFC's solution is simple and has been successfully used by other countries:
Honor commitments. Don't change rules midstream
MAP added that if rules are changed, new ones should be applied prospectively so as not to prejudice existing investments
To help solve electric power outages in 1990s, Japanese investors led by Marubeni formed San Roque Power Corp.
Invested huge amount of capital, imported machinery to generate about 400 megawatts of electricity
On government's promise of exemption from payment of value-added taxes (VAT)
At that time, it took $1 million to generate one megawatt
Now cost has doubled to $2 million per megawatt
Benefits of VAT exemption are enjoyed not just by investors but also by power consumers
Without exemption, VAT paid to government would be passed on to consumers who would thus have to pay higher power rates
Procedurally, San Roque was first required by government to pay VAT and then to apply for refund in BIR
Devil, as saying goes, is in details -- and here's where JFC's lament starts
Under law (RA 8424), application for VAT refund is required to be filed in BIR
If BIR rejects application, or fails to act on it within 120 days, applicant has 30 days to appeal to Court of Tax Appeals (CTA)
Otherwise, VAT refund would be forfeited
San Roque filed its refund application with BIR on March 28, 2003
But even before lapse of 120 days, it filed judicial claim in CTA on April 10, 2003
This was accepted practice at that time -- to undergo both administrative refund process in BIR and judicial process in CTA simultaneously, instead of successively
Simultaneous filing was justified because at that time, law also required judicial claims for refund to be filed within two years from submission of VAT returns
This time-saving practice of simultaneous processing was allowed by both BIR and CTA in at least 20 previous refund cases
But once simultaneous recourse to CTA was availed of, BIR suspended its own processing
After appropriate hearings, CTA granted San Roque VAT refund
But unlike in previous cases in which BIR simply accepted CTA decisions, BIR appealed to Supreme Court
Arguing San Roque filed its judicial claim prematurely because it did not wait for 120 days to lapse before going to CTA
On Jan 12, 2011, First Division of high court unanimously dismissed appeal and ordered BIR to refund VAT
Holding that simultaneous processing was legally justified
However, BIR moved for reconsideration
This time court en banc, in split decision last Feb 12, reversed First Division
And held San Roque was not entitled to VAT refund because it should have first waited for lapse of 120 days in BIR before filing judicial claim in CTA
To this decision, San Roque filed its own motion for reconsideration that is still pending
CJP thinks JFC and MAP are not contesting wisdom of new decision
They are merely asking that it be applied prospectively to new refund applications
But not to San Roque and other similarly situated companies, which followed old practice of simultaneous processing of refund applications sanctioned earlier by BIR and CTA
CJP believes this stance is reasonable, fair and equitable
New rules in processing applications for VAT exemptions should be applied prospectively
Art. 4 of Civil Code states: '[L]aws shall have no retroactive effect, unless the contrary is provided' in law itself
To show good faith, earn confidence of investors and ultimately spread fruits of our stunning economic growth with poor
Government should heed call of World Bank, MAP and JFC

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes the doctrinal sequel to his B19 column (two weeks earlier on JFC's pained letter), now focusing on the San Roque Power VAT-refund saga as case-study of why retroactive rule-changes destroy investor trust -- anchored on Article 4 of the Civil Code. Applauding the economy's giant 7.8% leap for the first quarter of the year, the World Bank and the MAP (organization of top business executives) called for the conversion of this naked growth to inclusive growth, one that alleviates poverty and creates jobs for our masses. FDIs and hot money: to do that, MAP joined the JFC in urging our government to honor its commitments to regain its credibility and trustworthiness -- in this space two weeks ago (B19), CJ opined that trustworthiness is the reason FDIs have come in trickles to the Philippines but have been poured massively on Malaysia, Thailand, Singapore, Indonesia and other neighbors. FDIs are desired everywhere because, unlike 'hot money,' they are rooted in and stay for many decades in basic industries that spur inclusive growth -- yes, inclusive growth, not just naked economic growth, is the goal of all countries because it promotes the prosperity of both the rich and the poor, both capital and labor, both the entrepreneurs and the masses. Hot money is invested short term, like in the stock market, bonds or bank deposits that can flee as fast as they come in -- FDIs are long-term commitments; once invested, they cannot be withdrawn instantly; hot money is not necessarily bad -- it helps in the expansion of existing businesses and normally precedes the more desirable FDIs. To attract FDIs, the JFC's solution is simple and has been successfully used by other countries: 'Honor commitments. Don't change rules midstream'; MAP added that if rules are changed, the new ones should be applied prospectively so as not to prejudice existing investments. San Roque Power: to help solve the electric power outages in the 1990s, Japanese investors led by Marubeni formed San Roque Power Corp. -- they invested a huge amount of capital in the company, which imported machinery to generate about 400 megawatts of electricity, on the government's promise of exemption from the payment of VAT; at that time, it took $1 million to generate one megawatt -- now the cost has doubled to $2 million per megawatt. The benefits of VAT exemption are enjoyed not just by the investors but also by the power consumers -- without the exemption, the VAT paid to the government would be passed on to the consumers who would thus have to pay higher power rates. Procedurally, San Roque was first required by the government to pay the VAT and then to apply for refund in the BIR -- the devil, as the saying goes, is in the details, and here's where JFC's lament starts; under the law (RA 8424), an application for VAT refund is required to be filed in the BIR; if the BIR rejects the application, or fails to act on it within 120 days, the applicant has 30 days to appeal to the CTA -- otherwise, the VAT refund would be forfeited. San Roque filed its refund application with the BIR on March 28, 2003 -- but even before the lapse of the 120 days, it filed a judicial claim in the CTA on April 10, 2003; this was the accepted practice at that time -- to undergo both the administrative refund process in the BIR and the judicial process in the CTA simultaneously, instead of successively; the simultaneous filing was justified because at that time, the law also required judicial claims for refund to be filed within two years from the submission of the VAT returns; this time-saving practice of simultaneous processing was allowed by both the BIR and the CTA in at least 20 previous refund cases -- but once simultaneous recourse to the CTA was availed of, the BIR suspended its own processing. After appropriate hearings, the CTA granted San Roque the VAT refund -- but unlike in the previous cases in which the BIR simply accepted the CTA decisions, the BIR appealed to the SC, arguing that San Roque filed its judicial claim prematurely because it did not wait for the 120 days to lapse before going to the CTA; on Jan 12, 2011, the First Division of the high court unanimously dismissed the appeal and ordered the BIR to refund the VAT, holding that simultaneous processing was legally justified. Reconsideration: however, the BIR moved for reconsideration -- this time the court en banc, in a split decision last Feb 12, reversed the First Division and held that San Roque was not entitled to the VAT refund because it should have first waited for the lapse of the 120 days in the BIR before filing its judicial claim in the CTA; to this decision, San Roque filed its own motion for reconsideration that is still pending. CJ thinks JFC and MAP are not contesting the wisdom of the new decision -- they are merely asking that it be applied prospectively to new refund applications, but not to San Roque and other similarly situated companies, which followed the old practice of simultaneous processing of refund applications sanctioned earlier by the BIR and the CTA; CJ believes this stance is reasonable, fair and equitable -- new rules in processing applications for VAT exemptions should be applied prospectively; Art. 4 of the Civil Code states: '[L]aws shall have no retroactive effect, unless the contrary is provided' in the law itself; to show good faith, earn the confidence of investors and ultimately spread the fruits of our stunning economic growth with the poor, the government should heed the call of the World Bank, MAP and JFC.
